message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact download/upload speeds you’re getting right now.  
But you can quickly find out yourself with a few simple steps:

---

## 1️⃣ Use a Web‑Based Speed Test

The easiest way is to visit a site that runs a speed test in your browser:

| Site | How to use |
|------|------------|
| **speedtest.net** (by Ookla) | Go to <https://www.speedtest.net>, click “Go” and wait for the test to finish. |
| **fast.com** (by Netflix) | Go to <https://fast.com> – it automatically starts a download test and shows you the speed. |
| **speedof.me** | Go to <https://speedof.me> – it runs a quick test and displays download, upload, and ping. |

These sites will give you:

- **Download speed** (Mbps)
- **Upload speed** (Mbps)
- **Ping / latency** (ms)

---

## 2️⃣ Run a Command‑Line Test (Windows)

If you prefer a terminal‑based test, you can use the free **speedtest‑cli** tool.  
Below are two ways to get it running on Windows:

### A. Using PowerShell + `curl` (no extra installs)

```powershell
# Download a 100 MB test file from Hetzner and time the download
$start = Get-Date
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin -OutFile C:\Temp\hetzner_test.bin
$end = Get-Date
$elapsed = ($end - $start).TotalSeconds
$bytes = (Get-Item C:\Temp\hetzner_test.bin).Length
$mbps = ($bytes / 1e6) / $elapsed * 8
Write-Host "Download speed: $([math]::Round($mbps,2)) Mbps"
```

> **What it does**  
> 1. Downloads a 100 MB file from a fast server.  
> 2. Measures how long it takes.  
> 3. Calculates the average speed in Mbps.

> **Limitations**  
> - Only measures download speed.  
> - Depends on the chosen server’s load and distance.

### B. Installing and using `speedtest-cli`

If you have Python and `pip` available, you can install the official CLI:

```powershell
# Install speedtest-cli (requires Python & pip)
pip install speedtest-cli

# Run a full test
speedtest-cli
```

> **What it does**  
> - Finds the best server automatically.  
> - Reports download, upload, and ping.  
> - Gives you a more accurate picture than a single file download.

---

## 3️⃣ Quick One‑Liner (if you just want a rough idea)

```powershell
# One‑liner that downloads a 10 MB file and prints speed
$start = Get-Date; Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://speed.hetzner.de/10MB.bin -OutFile C:\Temp\10MB.bin; $end = Get-Date; $elapsed = ($end - $start).TotalSeconds; $bytes = (Get-Item C:\Temp\10MB.bin).Length; $mbps = ($bytes / 1e6) / $elapsed * 8; Write-Host "≈$([math]::Round($mbps,2)) Mbps"
```

---

## 4️⃣ What to Look For

| Metric | Typical Values (Home Broadband) | What It Means |
|--------|---------------------------------|---------------|
| **Download** | 10 – 100 Mbps (or higher for fiber) | How fast you can stream, download files, etc. |
| **Upload** | 1 – 20 Mbps | Important for video calls, uploads, gaming. |
| **Ping** | < 50 ms | Lower ping = smoother online gaming, video calls. |

---

### Bottom Line

- **Web sites** (speedtest.net, fast.com) are the quickest and most reliable for most users.  
- **PowerShell** or **speedtest‑cli** give you a quick terminal alternative if you prefer not to open a browser.  

Run one of the methods above, and you’ll see your current internet speed in a few seconds. If you need help interpreting the results or troubleshooting slow speeds, let me know!
